#322. A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure

The midterms are over, and the next big fight could be over permitting reform.

A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years.

The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.

The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.

So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense.)

One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.

The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.

Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.

Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.

A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.

Another report, from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.

But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.

“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.

This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.

In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.

Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

Huge grid-scale batteries are thriving, but smaller residential systems have lagged.

These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.

New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid.

#321. Agility Robotics' Nasdaq debut invites scrutiny of humanoid robot market

US leader in deploying humanoid robots goes public on the Nasdaq stock exchange.

Humanoid robots remain unproven at scale and have not yet achieved widespread commercialization, compared with industrial robots that have decades of proven track records in warehouses and factories. That frank acknowledgment is among the risks outlined in a securities filing by Agility Robotics—the first dedicated developer of humanoid robots to become a publicly traded company in the United States.

The robotics company, headquartered in Salem, Oregon, previously became the first to achieve full-time commercial deployment of humanoid robots at a customer warehouse in 2024. Now, Agility’s public listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange as of November 5 has come with financial disclosures detailing how the company plans to build a business around renting out or selling humanoid robots to perform manual labor.

“When we are doing robots as a service, it is much lower risk for customers to use it because they are getting a return on investment on day one,” Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility Robotics, told Ars. “Because they’re paying a rate that is comparable to the human labor rate, and that makes the economics pretty straightforward.”

Agility is one of many startups attempting to commercialize humanoid robots. But the company has stood out from the competition through its lead in deploying and operating Digit humanoid robots with multiple customers, including the warehouses of logistics company GXO, the South Carolina factory of German automotive manufacturer Schaeffler, and the automotive production lines of Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. As Agility’s very first customer, GXO announced it would expand deployments of Digit robots beyond a warehouse in Georgia to additional facilities in North Carolina and Tennessee.

The filings accompanying Agility’s journey toward becoming a publicly traded company—based on a merger with a special purpose acquisition company—also provide a rare look at the business prospects and potential unit economics of humanoid robots. Most of its startup competitors remain privately held companies that have not been nearly as forthcoming.

Another exception has been China’s humanoid robotics company Unitree, which opened its books when it went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange STAR Market in August 2026.

Agility described the “illustrative unit economics” for both its “robots-as-a-service” subscription business and an “ownership model,” which would involve corporate clients purchasing robots outright, in an S-4 registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on September 4.

With the subscription model, customers would pay a one-time cost of about $25,000 per robot for delivery and deployment to a work site, along with a recurring monthly fee of $8,500 for software and maintenance.

Customers can also purchase the robot’s hardware outright for a one-time payment of $200,000, along with another one-time cost of $20,000 for delivery and deployment. But that still comes with an annual subscription fee of $36,000 for software and maintenance, or about $3,000 per month.

In exchange for renting or purchasing the robots, customers would get access to the latest Agility robot, known as Digit 5, starting in 2027. The bipedal robot has swappable end-effector “hands,” can lift up to 50-pound loads, and can perform more than 20 hours of work in a 24-hour period with the help of a fast-charging battery system.

The fast-charging battery technology provided by the UK-based company Nyobolt requires just nine minutes to deliver 90 minutes of robot runtime. “We worked with them for well over a year to design the pack that goes in our robot,” Hurst told Ars. “So the battery pack is fully custom and is ours, and we have the exclusive agreement with Nyobolt around using their [battery] chemistry in humanoid robots.”

The Digit 5 also comes with an onboard safety system that enables it to detect humans moving nearby and take appropriate actions, like standing still or squatting to minimize the risk of harm. That could unlock more opportunities to deploy Digit 5 beyond the confines of isolated work cells within warehouses and factories, said Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer at Agility, in a previous conversation with Ars.

During a presentation for analysts and investors on October 6, Agility’s chief financial officer, Michael Beer, described the Digit subscription model as allowing customers to replace $200,000 in annual labor costs with $100,000 in annual robot costs, while buying a Digit robot outright could replace $1.1 million in labor costs with about $400,000 in robot costs over five years.

Meanwhile, Agility described its own annual operating costs per robot as being $15,000 to provide the necessary software and maintenance, along with a one-time cost of $15,000 for Agility to initially deploy each robot.

The robotics company also estimated each Digit v5 humanoid robot as initially costing Agility $150,000 based on the bill of materials. Each robot is estimated to have a useful operational lifespan of about five years.

But Agility anticipates that bill of materials cost falling to $75,000 per robot once it ramps up to annual production of 1,000 robots, and eventually $30,000 per robot if the company can produce 10,000 robots per year. The company plans to gradually ramp up production at its RoboFab manufacturing facility in Oregon.

When balancing such business costs versus revenue, Agility anticipates that it could earn about $500,000 per robot on an annual basis through the subscription model, and about $400,000 per robot each year if a customer purchases the Digit robots outright while paying ongoing software and maintenance fees.

The subscription revenue calculations disclosed in Agility’s S-4 filing were based on an unidentified customer’s $300 million order covering 1,000 Digit 5 robots over a three-year subscription contract.

However, such a customer order does not mean Agility is guaranteed to earn $300 million, because the contract requires the robotics company to deliver on certain “contractual milestones, product features and specifications.”

The robotics company’s financial disclosures also bluntly state that “Agility has incurred net losses since inception and expects to continue to incur operating and net losses for the foreseeable future.” In 2025, the company earned just $1.8 million in revenue against $140 million in operating loss, which shows it’s still in the early stages of building a sustainable business.

Agility said it continues to devote “substantially all of its resources to research, development, and commercialization of its humanoid robot,” while continuing to expand the RoboFab manufacturing facility. On October 21, Agility also announced plans to build a new facility in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, for supporting Digit robot deployments and further developing the robot’s software and AI.

Beyond the challenges of building its own business, Agility’s financial disclosures also cautioned that “competition in the humanoid and robotics market is intensifying rapidly, with well-funded entrants including Boston Dynamics, Tesla, Apptronik, Figure AI, 1X Technologies, Sanctuary AI, Hexagon, and NEURA Robotics, among others, actively developing competing humanoid systems.”

Many of those companies have advantages, such as “significantly greater brand recognition, customer relationships, and financial, technical, manufacturing, and other resources,” Agility’s S-4 filing acknowledged. It also listed business risks involving uncertain AI-driven robotic performance in the real world, safety issues in sharing workspaces with human workers, changing regulations, and cybersecurity threats.

Still, Agility co-founder Hurst described a large potential market with “millions of unfilled roles” involving manual tasks that would typically require higher-cost but relatively low-skilled human labor. Within the next year, Hurst expects multiple Agility customers to be sharing videos of the Digit robots “just very boringly doing their work” to the point where “all of the excitement and hype and novelty of humanoids has worn off.”

“It’ll look a bit like the dawn of the automotive market, and different companies will have different niches—some companies will build the Ford F-150 and some companies will build a Mazda Miata,” Hurst told Ars. “There’s going to be a bunch of different niches for multi-purpose human-centric machines like these.”

Although Hurst sees Agility’s path eventually leading to a general-purpose autonomous robot in the future, he has consistently dismissed the idea of any company immediately deploying humanoid robots to riskier and less structured environments, like people’s homes. “Digit 5 is not going to walk into your living room and do dishes and stuff like that,” he said. “Nobody is.”

Whatever happens with Agility’s journey in the coming years, it will be instructive for anyone interested in the broader trajectory of the humanoid robot industry.

#320. Sony re-releases 80s Walkman headphones with a modern twist, and I got to try them

Halloween may be over, but that isn't stopping Sony from performing their second resurrection in less than a month.

Following the rebirth of the Walkman (starting at an eye-watering $1,899.99), Sony is launching the Sony MDR-3R wired headphones. It's a modern take on the headphones that launched with the original Walkman. (You may also recognize them as the headphones Max wears in Stranger Things.) I got to try these new headphones ahead of their release, and they sound surprisingly good.

The new USB-C version of the retro headphones brings modern tech to the original Sony MDR-3 Walkman headphones, but the classic '80s design is the same. And unlike the Walkman 2.0, you won't have to shell out thousands if you want to live out your analog dreams: the headphones are available at Amazon and Sony for $59.99.

For this release, Sony's also rolling out an appropriate collaboration: a Stranger Things edition of the headphones will launch in honor of Stranger Things Day on Nov. 6. They feature an exclusive design with red and black ear cushions, plus a Stranger Things engraving on the headband. The price point is also slightly higher, at $79.99.

The retro Sony MDR-3R headphones are available at major retailers, including Amazon and Sony, for $59.99. Included with the headphones is two pairs of swappable ear cushions in blue and orange. Unlike the original version, they come with a USB-C connection and an in-line remote on the cable for playback controls, as well as a built-in mic for phone calls.

The Stranger Things edition comes with red and black ear cushions, while the standard version comes with blue and orange. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

First things first — I can confirm that listening to "Running Up That Hill" does hit different on these headphones.

Before I get into the sound, I also want to note that I was complimented on the look of these headphones three different times while testing them out. In the dozens of headphones I've tested, that's never happened before — and I've tried the Nothing headphones.

As for how they actually sound, Sony went for a similar profile to the OG version, using the same 23mm driver units found on the original headphones. Naturally, some re-engineering took place to give these headphones the benefits of modern audio tech. I will say — I was surprised by how clear the sound came through. Sure, it doesn't have the greatest depth, but I don't need that from these retro on-ear headphones.

The other huge benefit? While they can handle a range of genres, listening to music from the 70s and 80s on these just feels right. Never has Queen's "Cool Cat" felt so funky or has Billy Joel seemed so in a "New York State of Mind." Don't even get me started on the Talking Heads. I also discovered, while listening to Pat Benatar's "Hit Me With Your Best Shot," that these headphones can get really loud, so proceed with caution.

As expected, they did experience some sound leakage — my roommate sitting a few feet away from me could hear Pat wailing "fire away" clearly as I tested the limit of the headphones, but even at normal volumes, she could tell I was listening to something, even if she couldn't quite identify what. There were also some issues with sound leakage on calls. When FaceTiming my girlfriend, she said she heard herself speaking (even as I had the volume low), but she stipulated that it was an issue she experiences with AirPods-wearing friends, too.

All told, these aren't your premium headphones — but they're not trying to be. They're a fun way to lean into a very particular (very cool!) aesthetic, while getting a decent listening experience. They're certainly meant to be an eye-catching accessory. With no ability to fold or a carrying case, you better be ready to show them off wherever you go.

#318. The Download: Texas’s fragile AI boom and energy policy shifts

Plus: America’s data center boom has hit a political wall.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat, Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor, and Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. They won after making data centers a central issue on the campaign trail.

The swings could spell trouble for hyperscalers with ambitious plans in the state. They also add to growing anxiety that America’s AI buildout could stall.

Here’s how the election results could reshape AI’s future.

Democrats have taken control of both the House and the Senate, but we probably won’t see major federal climate and energy legislation while Trump remains president. The midterm elections could, however, be a big deal for energy at the state and local level.

The results could shape everything from the state grid and data center development to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emissions.

Find out what the midterms could mean for the future of US energy.

On November 9, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). It’s a plan that could start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved. But some environmental groups oppose the bill, or parts of it.

Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov is, at least unofficially, a spy. Once a month, he drives to the frontline in a VW van equipped with radio hardware, roof antennas, and devices that monitor drones. Over several days, he searches the skies for transmissions that can help Ukrainian troops.

Drones define this brutal conflict, and most rely on the radio communications Flash has obsessed over since childhood. Though now a civilian, the former officer has taken it upon himself to inform his country’s defense on all matters related to radio.

#317. Burger King’s viral holiday advent calendar is back: How to buy the internet’s mini obsession

TL;DR: Burger King is launching its 2026 holiday advent calendar. Sold exclusively on BKAdventCalendar.com, 110 calendars will be available daily from Nov. 16-20, while supplies last.

Burger King announced that its limited-edition holiday advent calendar is returning for its third consecutive run. Unlike standard chocolate-filled boxes, the 2026 BK Advent Calendar lets buyers build a fully functional miniature Burger King restaurant over 12 days.

The box retails for $19.54 (a nod to the year the chain was founded in 1954). The catch? It is incredibly tough to actually get your hands on this viral product. Only 110 units will drop each day at 12 p.m. ET from Nov. 16-20, exclusively via BKAdventCalendar.com while supplies last.

The last two calendars sold out in under five minutes, so fans are encouraged to mark their calendars before this year's drop is gone for good. In fact, you can text “ADVENT” to 251-251 to get a reminder when the first drop goes live.

Behind each of the calendar's 12 doors is a piece of the Burger King experience, just mini. From fan-favorite menu items like the Whopper to restaurant details like the King's Booth and a soda fountain, the calendar packs some of the brand's most recognizable elements into an extremely festive package.

And on Day 12, the pieces combine to form a complete miniature storefront, accompanied by a $5 BK digital coupon code for Royal Perks members.

"We know Guests will be excited that for the third year in a row, the Advent Calendar is back, and it's the best one ever," said Joel Yashinsky, Chief Marketing Officer, Burger King US&C. "These limited-edition Advent Calendars sell out fast, and we know our Guests are always looking for more holiday fun from BK. So this year, fans can build their very own BK restaurant, complete with a mini-Whopper, nuggets, and other items that make BK feel like BK. It's our one-of-a-kind way to celebrate the season, and we can't wait for families to bring a little BK home for the holidays!"

Joseph Green is the Global Shopping Editor for Mashable. He covers VPNs, headphones, fitness gear, dating sites, streaming, and shopping events like Black Friday and Prime Day.

Joseph is also Executive Editor of Mashable's sister site, AskMen.

#316. Poland arrests 4 accused of spying for Russia

Poland has charged four people with espionage, saying they were sending information to Moscow. Two more have been accused of shipping military components to Russia.

Polish authorities said Thursday that they had arrested six people over alleged military component shipments to Russia, four of whom have been charged with espionage.

Investigators said the group illegally supplied Moscow with significant quantities of parts used to manufacture ammunition and weapons systems despite an embargo.

Four suspects, including the Russian woman, were charged with espionage and placed in pretrial detention for three months, Poland's Internal Security Agency (ABW) said. The other two are subject to non-custodial restrictions.

All six also face allegations of violating rules governing international trade in goods and technologies of strategic importance to national defense and international security.

"Russia is subject to a strict embargo in this area, and this operation was designed to circumvent it," Siemoniak told reporters.

The suspects are five Poles aged 25 to 52 and a 37-year-old Russian woman, intelligence coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak said.

#315. Pornhub traffic skyrocketed the morning of Election Day

Pornhub is one of the top-visited websites in the world. So, performing their civic duty on Election Day doesn't stop Americans from watching explicit content.

It seems that the U.S. (at least, half the states where Pornhub isn't blocked) woke up with an insatiable urge to watch porn, as traffic at 5 a.m. was 22 percent higher on Nov. 3 compared to an average day. (All visitor times are adjusted by local time, according to Pornhub.) The above-average numbers continued until around 4 p.m., before most polls closed.

For the next couple of hours, traffic dipped at most 10 percent below average. In the early evening, perhaps after many people voted, it rose up again to slightly above average. By 10 p.m., though, it was back down — maybe because they were watching Steve Kornacki deliver the election results instead.

Pornhub has blocked itself in many states due to age-verification laws, so there's no data on whether people in key battlegrounds like Georgia, Texas, Florida, and the Carolinas opted to watch porn on Tuesday.

But in Washington, D.C., Pornhub traffic was a staggering 43 percent higher than average in the morning and 25 percent in the afternoon, suggesting that political staffers may have had to let off a little steam. (It's less staggering than in 2022, however, when Pornhub traffic doubled in D.C.)

Wisconsin also saw a bigger-than-average day on Pornhub, with 20 percent higher traffic in the morning and 16 percent in the afternoon. Michigan and Ohio, with their highly-watched races, saw modest increases (8 percent and 5 percent, respectively).

See how other states fared on Election Day in Pornhub's blog post.

#313. Motorola's new Signature 27 has it all if you can stomach the $1,600 price tag

It has all the bells and whistles (and cameras).

Motorola is patching a hole in its US lineup with a non-folding flagship phone, but the pricing puts this device dangerously close to the company’s expensive tablet-style foldable. The long-rumored Motorola Signature 27 is real, featuring top-of-the-line specs, a super-bright OLED screen, and a ton of cameras. But all this high-end hardware won’t come cheap in the age of AI. Motorola’s new flagship smartphone will run a whopping $1,600 when it arrives later this month.

The Signature 27 is a new take on flagship smartphones from Motorola, leaving behind the middling legacy of the Edge series. However, you’ll still immediately clock this as a Motorola device due to its distinctive use of materials and Pantone colors. The phone is metal, ceramic, and glass, but the backs are textured polycarbonate. The device comes in Coal Smoke (black) or Capulet Olive (green) colors. The former has a “tactical weave” finish inspired by automotive design, and the latter is “textile-inspired.”

This device will include the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the most powerful mobile chip Qualcomm offers right now. While some smartphones have flirted with 16GB of memory, that’s less common these days. The Signature 27 will have 12GB like Samsung’s base model flagships. However, there’s not going to be an upgrade option for more. You will, however, get a generous 512GB of storage.

The phone is fairly thin in most places, but it tapers outward near the camera module. It’s easy to see why Moto needed a little more space up there with four image sensors. Note: That’s not four cameras. There are three standard cameras: a 50MP primary, a 50MP ultrawide, and a 200MP 3x optical zoom (100x digital zoom). Joining the cameras is an event-based vision sensor (EVS) to power a feature called Action Shot.

The action sensor measures changes in light at a pixel level, which makes it ideal for tracking moving subjects. Action Shot will turn on automatically when the phone detects a lot of movement in the frame, but you can also activate it manually. Motorola’s cameras have long struggled to capture moving subjects clearly, so it’ll be interesting to see if the EVS fixes that.

If you’ve been thinking about a smaller phone, the Signature 27 isn’t for you. This phone sports a sizable 6.8-inch OLED screen with a 120Hz refresh rate. This is a tandem OLED panel, which uses stacked pixels to increase brightness. Moto claims the Signature 27 can hit an impressive 12,000 nits of peak brightness, which is four times higher than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (and the highest of any smartphone). A possible drawback is that tandem OLEDs tend to have a somewhat uneven appearance at low brightness with solid colors, but we haven’t seen the Signature 27 in person yet to say whether or not that’s the case here.

A display like that could really drain your battery, but the Signature 27 has capacity to spare. The 7,000 mAh silicon-carbon cell is the largest of any mainstream smartphone, 1,000 mAh larger than the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Motorola estimates it could last two days on a charge, and it won’t take long to refill. With a compatible USB-C charger (not included), the Signature 27 can reach speeds up to 90W. Moto claims up to 12 hours of usage in 12 minutes of charging.

The Motorola Signature 27 will ship with Android 17 and Moto’s Hello UI customizations. The company promises seven years of OS updates, on par with Samsung and Google.

This will be a full Gemini Intelligence device, entitling it to Google’s most expansive list of AI features. Moto says the Signature 27 will get Google’s agentic app control, Create My Widget, Sign-to-Text, and Rambler voice input. However, these features will arrive “in the coming months,” as most of those features are still limited to Pixel phones.

Moto is still offering a parallel set of AI features on its phones. Features like Catch me up (notification summaries) and Pay Attention (meeting notes) are still supported, but the company appears to have dropped the Moto AI branding. Instead, these are all part of Motorola Qira, an AI platform that also connects your Motorola phone to Lenovo computers.

Credit: Motorola Credit: Motorola

Motorola does not intend to ship a version of the Signature 27 with GrapheneOS preloaded, so it’ll be up to buyers to install it. Details on that process will come at a later date, but it should be similar to Pixel phones—unlock the bootloader, flash the software, and enjoy.

Some months back, the Graphene team revealed the first device in its Moto collaboration would be priced above Pixels, and that certainly checks out. Motorola is asking $1,600 for the Signature 27, putting it above even the high-end flagship phones from Samsung and Apple. It’s also within $300 dollars of foldable phones like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Motorola’s own Razr Fold (both $1,900 MSRP). Even the iPhone Duo is only $400 more than Moto’s new flagship slab.

Moto hasn’t announced any carrier partnerships yet. So you’ll have to buy the device directly from Motorola, Best Buy, or Amazon when it goes on sale on November 26. Preorders will be available starting November 19 if you are so inclined.

#312. Tumblr is having a fandom renaissance amid the AO3 outage

When Archive of Our Own (AO3) went offline on Oct. 29 for an extended maintenance period, millions of fanfiction readers suddenly found themselves with a lot more free time. But fandom doesn't simply disappear when its favorite website goes down. It finds somewhere else to congregate.

And apparently, that somewhere is Tumblr, an old familiar haunt for millennial fans.

According to data shared with Mashable by Tumblr, the blogging platform has seen a significant increase in new users since AO3 went offline. Between Oct. 29 and Nov. 2, new sign-ups increased 49 percent compared to the previous two weeks. Among users ages 18 to 25, that number jumped to 75 percent.

Tumblr also reported an increase in daily active users, though it did not provide a specific percentage. Meanwhile, the biggest increase in daily users joining Tumblr Communities, the platform's dedicated spaces for shared interests, reached 63 percent.

In other words, AO3's temporary absence appears to be giving one of fandom's longtime gathering places a boost.

"Fandom has always had a home on Tumblr, and we're glad to be a place fans can gather while AO3 recovers," Ari Levine, Tumblr's head of brand marketing and partnerships, said in a statement. "We've offered to help, and we're rooting for the OTW's volunteers and hope to see it back soon."

The numbers offer a glimpse into how fandom communities are navigating AO3's extended downtime. The fanfiction archive, which is operated by the nonprofit Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), has become an essential part of online fandom culture, housing millions of fan-created stories across thousands of fandoms. Its temporary shutdown has left readers scrambling for alternative ways to access their favorite works and writers figuring out where to reconnect with their audiences.

For some, that means returning to Tumblr. Of course, Tumblr and AO3 have long existed alongside each other in the fandom ecosystem. Where AO3 provides an archive for fanworks, Tumblr has historically served as a place to discuss them, share recommendations, post fan art, and build communities around shared obsessions. It's where a reader might discover a new ship, find a fic recommendation, or follow an author whose work they love.

That relationship makes Tumblr a natural gathering place during AO3's absence. According to Tumblr, fans have been sharing fanfiction recommendations, reconnecting through fandom Communities, and commiserating over the outage.

What's particularly notable is the increase in younger users. Tumblr has been a fixture of internet fandom for well over a decade, but its 75 percent increase in sign-ups among 18- to 25-year-olds suggests that the current disruption may also be introducing a new generation of fans to the platform.

Still, the numbers don't necessarily mean Tumblr is experiencing a permanent resurgence. The company shared percentage increases rather than raw sign-up figures, and it's too early to know whether these new users will stick around once AO3 returns. The timing also doesn't establish that every new account was created because of the outage.

But the surge illustrates something about how online fandom works. Fan communities aren't confined to a single website, even when that website becomes central to how they participate. They exist across platforms, held together by the people who create, recommend, discuss, and share the stories they love.

AO3 may be where fans go to read the fic. But while it's offline, Tumblr is reminding them that fandom has always been about more than the archive.

#311. 6 Best VPN Services (2026), Tested and Reviewed

Hundreds of VPNs are at your disposal. They all want you to believe they’re the best VPN you can buy. All of them claim to have the biggest network or a no-logging policy. And they all promise your internet traffic is safe on the network of servers they’ve rented. Only some of them are telling the truth.

VPNs are only growing in popularity due to age-verification laws in the UK and in several states in the US. Even if you don’t want a VPN, you might need one. If you’re hesitant, I get it. VPN providers have been deep in murky waters for years, constantly caught lying about their practices, handing over user data that was never supposed to be logged, and serving as safe havens for large cybercriminal organizations.

I wanted to find the VPN services that actually work; the ones that keep their promises even in the face of potential prosecution, and the ones that have a proven track record of reliable performance. Some of the picks in this guide aren’t conventional, and some of the services I suggest you avoid might be controversial. But these are the top VPNs I’d use day to day.

Read our other VPN guides, including how to set up a VPN on your router and how to use a VPN to watch Netflix when you travel abroad.

If your looking to get a VPN deal, Proton, our top VPN pick (read more below), is running an early Black Friday sale: 75 percent off the regular price for two years. You can get Proton VPN Plus for $2.49 a month (regularly $10 a month); billed at $60 for 24 months. VPN Plus protects up to 10 devices and gives you access to more than 20,000 servers, plus it blocks ads, trackers, and malware. You can also snag one year of Proton Unlimited for $6.50 a month (regularly $13 a month); billed at $78 for 12 months, which adds Proton’s mail, calendar, and password manager software, plus 500 GB of cloud storage. We don’t know when this deal expires, but we imagine it will last through Cyber Monday.

What Does a VPN Do? And How Does It Work?

VPN stands for virtual private network. A VPN provides a tunnel through which all of your internet traffic passes. Instead of connecting to your internet service provider's servers, you connect to a VPN's server before connecting to the broader internet. Because most VPN services operate this way, your browsing data isn't stored, essentially making you anonymous online.

The linchpin in this system is a VPN protocol. Today, nearly all internet traffic is encrypted, but that encryption happens only after you've established a connection with a website. A VPN protocol encrypts traffic before it reaches the VPN server, adding extra security on untrusted networks like public Wi-Fi at a coffee shop or airport. It doesn't help much on your personal network unless there is an intruder.

By routing your traffic through a server in another location, you can also bypass geo-restrictions online, such as the content libraries available in different countries on Netflix or checking product availability in other regions of the world.

VPNs can also be important when connecting to public Wi-Fi. If you're doing anything remotely sensitive on your computer at a coffee shop, a VPN is a good idea to protect your personal data.

VPN prices vary widely, but most providers cost around $10 per month for a monthly plan. Pricing changes if you buy several months at once, and it gets even more complicated with full security suites, such as those offered by Nord Security and Proton.

Most prominent VPN services offer multi-month or even multiyear discounts. These plans are often the best way to get your foot in the door, but some VPNs have recently faced class-action lawsuits over their auto-renewal practices. Although a handful of lawsuits have been filed, that doesn't mean these services necessarily engaged in illegal practices.

Free VPNs exist, as well, but you should avoid most of them. Some restrictive free plans from Proton and Windscribe are useful, but you should approach most free VPNs with skepticism.

You'll come across a few of these terms in this guide as you generally shop for a VPN. Here's what they mean.

Split tunneling: Allows you to choose which apps use the VPN tunnel. Useful if you want some apps (like your browser) to use the VPN tunnel but not others.

Kill switch: A security feature in VPNs that will disable your internet connection if the VPN connection drops. A kill switch can prevent internet traffic from leaking if the VPN fails.

IP and domain block list: A list of IP addresses or domain names that are blocked inside the VPN tunnel. Some VPNs offer Domain Name System (DNS) blocking, too, which can block ads served from particular DNS servers.

Static IP: Most VPNs assign you a random IP address, or even rotate the IP address while you’re connected. If you need external access to your network with a network-wide VPN, you'll need a static IP address.

Port forwarding: Allows you to forward a port on your private network, bypassing the VPN tunnel. Useful when you need external network access with a network-wide VPN, such as running a media server.

NetShield: A feature specific to Proton VPN that blocks ads and trackers while connected to the VPN. Other services, such as Windscribe and NordVPN, offer similar features.

Dark web monitoring: A feature available in some VPNs, such as NordVPN and ProtonVPN, that will monitor the dark web for your email address or other personal information. You'll be notified if the information shows up on the dark web or as part of a breach.

DAITA: A feature of Mullvad VPN that will introduce background noise to your connection, combating AI-assisted network analysis. Windscribe, NordVPN, and ProtonVPN offer similar features.

Short of a few exceptions, VPNs are legal around the world. That includes the US, UK, Canada, Australia, the EU, South Africa, and many countries in Central and South America. Places such as North Korea and Turkmenistan have VPN bans in place, but due to the extreme censorship in those countries, it's hard to verify what laws are on the books (and how they're enforced). You can probably guess the North Korean government's stance on bypassing censorship, though.

For everyone else, VPN legality only comes into play based on which VPN you use and what you use it for. Countries such as India and Russia call for compliance with the government, forcing providers like NordVPN to shut down servers in those regions. And, regardless of what country you're in, engaging in illegal activity while connected to a VPN is still illegal.

Update November 2026: We’ve added a mention of an early Black Friday deal for Proton VPN.

Proton VPN (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is the best VPN you can buy. Its Plus service was the fastest I tested across the US and UK. It has a generous free plan if you'd like to try it out first. The features are unmatched, and the pricing is excellent, especially if you bundle Proton VPN with the company's other software (Proton Unlimited). After testing all of these services, Proton is what I personally use now.

What sent Proton over the edge was its commitment to transparency. It has maintained a transparency report since 2017, undergone third-party audits annually since 2022, and open-sourced its applications five years ago. That last bit is huge, as bugs within the application can pose a security risk, and handing those applications over to the open-source community can surface those bugs much faster. There are no real compromises here, with features like split tunneling, port forwarding, and double-hop connections.

Black Friday is a good time to sign up for Proton VPN. The company is offering 75 percent off the regular price for two years.

NordVPN has a long history, and it's one of the most prominent VPN services on the market. It comes with one of the largest VPN networks available, enough features to make Surfshark blush, and decent (though not the best) speeds. It's a little more expensive than I'd hoped for, but that's the price you pay for such an extensive network and feature set.

That feature set is where NordVPN stands apart. Its Basic plan will get you access to the VPN, but I recommend going with at least the Plus plan. It opens up an ad blocker and gives you access to one of the best password managers around, NordPass.

These extras wouldn't mean much on their own, but the core of NordVPN is still an excellent VPN service. It's been on the bleeding edge of VPN security and features for years, and that hasn't changed.

You should generally avoid free VPNs, but Windscribe is one of the few worth considering. You get 10 GB of data across 10 server locations and unlimited connections, and you can even unlock more data if you refer friends or post on social media about Windscribe. There are a few similar offers from services like Proton, but Windscribe provides a pleasant on-ramp for subscribing.

If you do decide to pay, you can build your own plan. Unlimited data runs an extra $3 per month, and you can add server locations for an extra $1 per server per month. It's fantastic. Most people don't need VPN servers in Ghana, Cambodia, and Peru, so rather than charge for all those locations, you can pick out your locations piecemeal. If you want everything, that's available at a discounted rate, too.

The pricing model is what sets Windscribe apart, but it's an excellent VPN in its own right. It offers additional packet obfuscation to combat network analysis, and it's loaded with features like split tunneling and port forwarding. It's fast, too, dropping just 15.6 percent of my speed when connected in the US.

Like the other providers I've included, Windscribe has undergone a third-party audit. But unlike the other options, it's also been taken to court. Windscribe CEO Yegor Sak was personally charged with a crime in Greece in relation to a user's activity on Windscribe-operated servers, essentially tying activity on the network to Sak personally. It was dismissed. VPNs are subpoenaed all the time, but the fact that Windscribe wasn't able to produce logs even when the CEO of the company was facing criminal prosecution speaks volumes.

Windscribe added random hashed login in December 2025, which makes it possible to create an anonymous account. Windscribe doesn’t record the random hash, so if you lose it, you’ll also lose account access—but it can help to keep your identity private. This is similar to how Mullvad and IVPN handle accounts. Windscribe accepts cryptocurrency payments as well.

Any VPN worth its salt claims a no-logs policy, but almost all of them keep some logs. Those logs shouldn't have anything to do with your browsing data, and they should be anonymized, but most VPNs need to at least keep logs of information like your email and payment method. But not Mullvad.

Mullvad doesn't do multi-year subscriptions, referral links, or social sign-on. You generate an account number to sign up, and you add time to that account with the payment method of your choice, including a credit card, PayPal, crypto, or cold, hard cash (via mail). If you want to go through the hassle, you can stay fully anonymous in the eyes of Mullvad. If that wasn't enough, Mullvad even claims it was raided by Swedish police and still didn't produce logs.

It's not as fast as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark, but it's not bad, either—around a 24 percent drop in the US compared to 19 percent with Surfshark—and it lacks some features like port forwarding. But the pricing is good at roughly $6 a month, depending on exchange rates (Mullvad charges a flat €5 regardless of location).

While the built-in, free Bitdefender VPN is usable, it's too limited for what most people will want. The company's paid option, Bitdefender VPN Premium, gets you support for up to 10 devices, and it's plenty reliable and fast—without the data restrictions. Its biggest draw is its first-year price: it's only $30, which is a great value for a VPN like this. It goes up to $70 after the first year, though, which is a bit more expensive than ProtonVPN. But that first-year price comes out to just $2.92 per month, making it an especially good VPN for beginners to try.

ExpressVPN has had a rough few years, but it finally seems to be on solid footing. It was purchased a few years back for almost $1 billion by Kape Technologies, a firm that owns several VPNs, including CyberGhost and Private Internet Access. A revolving door of executives followed the sale, but ExpressVPN's leadership is solid enough now that it's worth recommending.

That's because the service itself hasn't degraded in the past few years. ExpressVPN is still insanely fast, packed with features, and dead-simple to use across desktop and mobile. It can go toe-to-toe with the top dogs, and it's always been able to. That hasn't changed.

However, I'm recommending it here due to recent changes ExpressVPN made to its membership options. Its core service is still intact, offering 10 simultaneous connections and full access to the ExpressVPN network. You can push higher, though, with the Advanced plan offering 12 connections and the Pro plan offering 14. The Advanced plan is best for most people, not only due to the higher connection limit but also because it comes with a password manager and 50 percent off one of ExpressVPN’s AirCove routers.

Surfshark: I've used Surfshark personally for a few years, and I'd still be using it if Proton didn't impress me so much. Surfshark is dead simple to use. It pops up and connects before swiftly getting out of my way so I can get on with my day. If you spring for a two-year plan, it's cheap. You can score over two years for around $54 with the Starter plan.

EventVPN: This is a free, ad-supported VPN from ExpressVPN. Ads and VPNs don't really mix, but EventVPN says it's able to offer a free service via Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) and Identifier for Advertisers (IDFA), basically allowing it to serve ads without harvesting your personal data. The problem is the pervasiveness of ads. A banner lives at the top of the app at all times, and you'll need to sit through a 30-second ad each time you connect or disconnect; a big problem when some servers post unreasonably slow speeds. I'll admit EventVPN is a unique concept, but I see nothing better than ProtonVPN or Windscribe for a free VPN service. And when it comes to the inconvenience of sitting through ads, it's straight-up worse.

PrivadoVPN: A popular option to recommend as a free VPN, offering a decent free service, with a handful of full-speed servers and 10 GB of data per month. You'll have to suffer through four—yes, four—redirects begging you to pay for a subscription before signing up, but the free plan works. The problem is how new PrivadoVPN is. There's no transparency report or audit available, and although the speeds are decent, they aren't as good as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark. PrivadoVPN isn't bad, but it's hard to recommend when Proton and Windscribe exist with free plans that are equally as good.

X-VPN is available on desktop, but it primarily shows up in results on the Apple App Store and Google Play, targeting mobile users with a free offering. X-VPN hasn't done anything explicitly wrong like Hola, but it has way too many inconsistencies to recommend. For starters, it uses a proprietary VPN protocol, which it obfuscates within the app. Proprietary protocols like NordVPN's NordLynx and ExpressVPN's Lightway are based on existing, open-source protocols. Further, X-VPN was highlighted in a Tech Transparency Project report about free VPNs with links to the Chinese government; X-VPN is based in Hong Kong. There's no smoking gun with X-VPN, but there doesn't need to be. The speeds aren't the best, the app lacks basic features like split tunneling, and the pricing for a paid plan is in line with top providers.

Functionally, a VPN should do two things: keep your internet speed reasonably fast, and actually protect your browsing data. That's where I focused my testing. Extra features, a comfy UI, and customization settings are great, but they don't matter if the core service is broken.

Speed testing requires spot-checking, as the time of day, the network you're connected to, and the specific VPN server you're using can all influence speeds. Because of that, I always set a baseline speed on my unprotected connection directly before recording results, and I ran the test three times across both US and UK servers. With those baseline drops, I spot-checked at different times of the day over the course of a week to see if the speed decrease was similar.

Security is a bit more involved. For starters, I checked for DNS, WebRTC, and IP leaks every time I connected to a server using Browser Leaks. I also ran brief tests sniffing my connection with Wireshark to ensure all of the packets being sent were secured with the VPN protocol in use.

#310. North Korea tells EU to 'mind its own business' on human rights

North Korea's UN mission has lashed out at the European Union over a draft UN resolution. Pyongyang has said the West does not have a monopoly on human rights.

North Korea responded to the European Union's draft United Nations resolution on human rights in the country by telling the bloc to "mind its own business," state media reported Thursday.

Pyongyang has long been accused by the UN and human rights advocates of committing human rights violations.

North Korea's UN mission said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency that the move was a "farce" and a "politically motivated provocation."

It said the resolution is "flagrantly distorting it's human rights policy," claiming that human rights are not "a monopoly of the West."

Referring to the protests in Europe, the North Korean mission said: "Streets are filled with demonstrators from all walks of life demanding such elementary rights as the rights to existence."

"The EU had better mind its own business, instead of hyping up the nonexistent 'human rights issues,'" it added.

The UN General Assembly has adopted a resolution condemning North Korea's human rights violations every year since 2005.

According to the South Korean Yonhap News Agency, Seoul has decided to co-sponsor the resolution proposed by the EU.

It is the fifth consecutive year that Seoul has done so, following a break from 2019 to 2021 under the liberal Moon Jae-in government.

The draft text is expected to be adopted by the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly later this month, before being submitted to the UN General Assembly for final approval.

#309. Kai Cenat wants to take his time with GTA 6

After waiting 13 years for a new Grand Theft Auto game, Kai Cenat plans to take his time with it.

The streamer has clarified his plans for GTA 6, telling fans that his playthrough will leave plenty of room to explore rather than race through the story. In a post on X, Cenat said he wants to be "fully immersed" in the game and encouraged his audience to enjoy it at their own pace, too.

"Don't want you guys to think your [sic] about to see me try to beat the story fast as hell," he wrote. "Not happening."

Instead, Cenat said he'll combine story missions with "high-level exploration," discovering new features and enjoying the game fans have spent more than a decade waiting for. As for how long he'll be live, he's leaving that open.

"I ain't coming off stream until I feel like it’s the right time," he wrote.

The update follows Cenat's announcement of a separate GTA marathon ahead of the new game's release. As Mashable reported earlier this week, he plans to stream GTA 3, Vice City, San Andreas, GTA 4, and GTA 5 in one sitting, with the broadcast scheduled to begin Nov. 5 at 3 p.m. ET on Twitch and YouTube.

For GTA 6, though, his message goes beyond what viewers should expect from his stream. Cenat also urged fans to make time for their own playthroughs, saying the internet moves quickly and people don't always appreciate good games while they're playing.

"Take time and really have fun!" he wrote.

Grand Theft Auto VI launches Nov. 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

#308. Shania Twain calls for equal pay and more diversity in country music

Shania Twain is standing up for others in country music.

The legendary star in the genre used her acceptance speech for the Equal Play Award at Sunday’s CMT Awards to call for more equity and diversity in the country music industry.

“When I wrote the phrase ‘Man I feel like a woman’ I honestly had no idea at the time it would become an undercurrent of a decades-long career,” she said, referring to one of her biggest hits. “It’s amazing how one statement can empower so many.”

The phrase, Twain said, “has been adopted by an array of fantastic communities all around the world and become a genuine path of power…which brings me so much joy.”

“I believe in an all-inclusive country music. We’re family,” Twain said. “This is a genre of music with a rich history that raised and nurtured my own songwriting and performance and recording career from childhood. Currently, the industry standard does a real disservice to this.”

Twain, who was presented the award by rapper Megan Thee Stallion, shouted out some of the diverse acts she is spotlighting on her “Queen of Me” tour this year, including Lily Rose, Lindsay Ell, Hailey Whitters, Mickey Guyton and others.

“I will continue to do my best as a trailblazer,” Twain said. “Together, let’s ensure all our fellow artists get equal play regardless of gender, age or race.”

She also performed acappella with the African American singing group, The BoykinZ, while presenting an award onstage. Twain connected with the group, who are sisters and rising country stars, after Kelly Clarkson surprised them recently by bringing Twain out to meet them during an episode of Clarkson’s daytime talk show.

#307. 2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He said going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

“We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher said. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he said.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.

#306. Amazon ditches GrubHub for Uber Eats, effective immediately

That's what Amazon is saying in a Thursday announcement about its new partnership with Uber's popular food delivery service.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

While the order receipt will come from Uber Eats, Amazon will handle everything else for Prime users ordering delivery. The order process and delivery alerts will also come from Amazon.

Amazon originally entered the food delivery business with Amazon Restaurants, which was an in-house service provided by the company. However, in 2019, Amazon shuttered Amazon Restaurants and opted to instead partner with food delivery companies.

In 2022, Amazon announced a new partnership with GrubHub, which provided Amazon Prime users with a free GrubHub+ subscription. Two years later, in 2024, Amazon and Grubhub extended their partnership, making the Grubhub+ membership an ongoing perk for Prime members.

With the UberEats deal, Amazon's relationship with GrubHub is coming to an end. Both Amazon and GrubHub have confirmed that the partnership between the two companies will end on Thursday.

Ditching GrubHub for UberEats makes sense for Amazon. Amazon Prime perks are there to encourage its customers to keep their paid subscription active. According to a report from Foodspark, Uber Eats has between 23 and 26 percent share of the U.S. food delivery market. GrubHub only captures between 6 and 8 percent. This makes the new Amazon Prime offering much more appealing to a larger portion of its customer base.

#305. Statehouse wins give Democrats new power to push clean energy

Democrats erased the GOP’s trifecta edge and gained new power over energy policy.

Before Tuesday’s election, Republicans held more governorships and state legislative seats than Democrats, along with an advantage in state trifectas—unified control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature.

That advantage has disappeared, clearing the path for more climate and clean energy legislation, according to analysts and advocates.

Democrats swept the vast majority of competitive races at the state level, flipping control of governors’ offices from Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada, and Texas.

Democrats have a 29-19 edge in governorships, with Kansas too close to call and Alaska likely to take a while to declare a winner.

The party is on track for a net gain of hundreds of legislative seats, potentially giving it control of more nationwide than Republicans for the first time in more than a decade. Going into the election, Republicans had 4,072 seats and Democrats held 3,257, according to MultiState, a research and lobbying firm. Democrats had a net gain of more than 350 seats on Tuesday and are likely to add several hundred more as results continue to be tabulated, according to MultiState.

Democrats won five new trifectas: Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, with Arizona likely to be the sixth once officials finish counting. Those additions would give the party 22 trifectas, with Republicans holding unified control in 18 states and nine with split control. Kansas is yet to be determined.

Republicans lost trifectas in Iowa, Georgia, Texas, New Hampshire, and Ohio. Before the election, Republicans had trifectas in 23 states, Democrats had 16, and 11 were under split control.

The implications for climate and energy policy are likely to be profound, said Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, an advocacy group.

“In the states, we had a generational political window shift to make people’s lives better, to lower costs, and to lower climate pollution at the same time,” she said in a conference call.

This was the “affordability election” with concerns about inflation and high energy prices, she said.

Newly elected lawmakers will enter office with energy policy proposals to address voter concerns, she said. She noted that renewable energy is less expensive than fossil fuels and can be developed quickly, promising rapid benefits for consumers. The growth of electric transportation reduces greenhouse gas emissions and shields consumers from the volatility of gasoline and diesel, she said.

Jay Inslee, former Democratic governor of Washington and a prominent advocate for climate and clean energy policies, urged lawmakers to seize this opportunity.

Inslee took a jab at President Donald Trump, calling him the election’s clear loser, even though he wasn’t on the ballot.

“The chief climate denier got his head handed to him,” Inslee said.

John Farrell, co-director of the Institute for Local Self-Reliance, a research and advocacy nonprofit, said in an interview that he is excited to see what comes next with the new trifectas.

“There is this growing sense that more accountability measures are needed in order to rein in [utility] rates, and that utility companies are central to that problem,” he said.

Farrell sees an opportunity for Wisconsin to catch up with neighboring states that have already established climate and clean energy agendas. He’s pleased that Democrats’ legislative majorities in Minnesota are large enough to give the party leeway to propose more ambitious policies. In Michigan, he is encouraged by residents calling for publicly owned utilities and pushing back against the influence of large utilities.

In the past, Farrell might have worried that utilities would stave off consumer-friendly policies by showering newly elected Democrats with campaign donations. But he thinks scenarios like this are less likely now because the public is wary of candidates they view as puppets for large companies. And some candidates have shown it’s possible to win without accepting money from utilities.

“We’re in a moment right now where there is enough scrutiny to make it harder for that sort of check-writing strategy to be successful,” he said.

Dan Gearino covers the business and policy of renewable energy and utilities, often with an emphasis on the midwestern United States. He is the main author of ICN’s Inside Clean Energy newsletter. He came to ICN in 2018 after a nine-year tenure at The Columbus Dispatch, where he covered the business of energy. Before that, he covered politics and business in Iowa and in New Hampshire. He grew up in Warren County, Iowa, just south of Des Moines, and lives in Columbus, Ohio.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#304. Spotify is coming to United's seatback screens

The streaming service's entire library of content will be available in the air.

Spotify is making it easier to stream music, podcasts and audiobooks on United Airlines flights. As part of a new collaboration with the airline, the company says that seatback screens on United planes equipped with Starlink satellite internet will soon have full access to Spotify's library of content, along with your personalized home screen and playlists.

To access your library, Spotify says you have to connect your phone to United's inflight Wi-Fi and then scan the QR code on your seatback screen. You'll then be prompted to log in, or if you're already logged in to your Spotify app, the screen will automatically load your Spotify profile. From there, based on the images Spotify shared, the seatback app seems to work similarly to the company's tablet apps. Connecting to Wi-Fi for Spotify is free, so you won't need to pay for an inflight internet pass.

Other airlines like American Airlines offer music streaming as a perk for customers, either through the seatback screen or by supporting free streaming on certain apps you already have on your device, so this isn't a first. The advantage of this Spotify integration is the opportunity to use the seatback screen instead of your phone if you want to watch a video podcast or music video. If you're used to downloading playlists or podcasts before a flight, not having to worry about that when you fly United is also helpful.

United began testing Starlink on flights at the beginning of 2025, and the airline now says that nearly half of its daily departures offer Starlink internet. If you regularly fly with the airline and are curious about trying the Spotify app, you can check whether your flight has Starlink internet through United's Starlink Wi-Fi Tracker.
